newsitem.title: GERMANY: Europe goes full steam ahead toward monetary union.
newsitem.headline: Europe goes full steam ahead toward monetary union.

text.p: European financial leaders, rallied by Chancellor Helmut Kohl of Germany, have made clear that Europe is moving toward monetary union with an unstoppable momentum, with the only question now which countries will make the grade.

Finance ministers addressing the gathering of some 800 bankers attending the annual European Banking Congress reaffirmed their commitment to creating a stable European currency by 1999 and said they were determined their countries would be in at the start.
European countries that want to meld their currencies into the planned "Euro" in 1999 are scrambling to meet economic targets on interest and exchange rateficits and public debt in the 1997 year.

Most are facing the greatest problems in meeting the fiscal targets, which call for budget deficits to run at a maximum of three percent of gross domestic product and public debt at a maximum of 60 percent of GDP.
Most experts expect Europe's two financial power houses, France and Germany, to form a core group around which several smaller nations will form the first club of monetary union.

Italy, not wanting to be left out, tried to keep its hopes alive of being in that group, announcing that its government had asked for the Italian lira to be readmitted to Europe's exchange rate mechanism.
"Our government has asked for the lira to re-enter the ERM," Antonio Fazio, Governor of the Bank of Italy, said in response to a question at the banking congress in Frankfurt.
The lira was forced out of the close-knit exchange rate system in 1992.

Spain's Economy Minister, Rodrigo de Rato, also keen to be in EMU at the start, said, "I believe by now there ought not to be many doubts ... in financial markets that Spain finds itself on the right track to convergence and monetary union."
French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis brushed aside worries that France's bid to cut its budget deficits to meet the Maastricht goal in 1997 was only a one-off effort.
"This effort is part of a strategy to cut the public deficit on a durable basis," he said.
Arthuis stressed that France intended to achieve long-term fiscal stability, adding that such discipline will be essential for the stability of the future European currency.
The French budget deficit would be within the three percent limit in 1997. France then intended to cut the deficit to 2.8 percent in 1998 and to below 2 percent by 2001.
